tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Write a procedure called finish that prints done. Display [word]. Then call finish, so the word is printed first.

tests.why: The word is printed first, then the procedure prints done. If you only see one line you have defined finish but never called it - defining a procedure does not run it.
A one letter word is printed just the same. If this failed you may have typed the word into the procedure instead of reading it with input().
input() hands back the whole line, so both words are printed together. The word done never changes, so it belongs inside the procedure.

tasks.fb: A procedure is a named block of code you can run whenever you like. Writing def finish(): only creates it - the line finish() is what runs it.

teach.say: def gives a block of code a name. The indented lines do nothing until a line calls that name.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two words, one on each line. Write a procedure called rule that prints =====. Call rule, so the first line is the rule. Then display the first word on the next line. Then call rule again. Then display the second word on the next line. Then call rule a third time.
brief: The same procedure prints all three rules.

tests.why: There is a rule above, between and below the two words, so rule() is called three times.
Different words, same layout. If the words came out in the wrong order, check you stored the first input() before reading the second.
Exactly five equals signs each time. Four or six will not match, and a rule printed on the same line as a word will not either.

tasks.fb: The point of a procedure is that the code for the rule is written once. If you copied print('=====') out three times you have not used a subprogram at all.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two words, one on each line. Write a procedure called show that takes one word and prints value [that word]. Call show once for each word, in the order they were typed.
brief: Nothing but those two lines is printed.
One space after the word value.

tests.why: The parameter is what makes one procedure work for both words. If both lines say the same word, you printed the same variable twice instead of passing each one in.
Nothing about the word is written inside the procedure - it arrives as the parameter.
The same word twice should print twice. If only one line appeared you may have skipped the second call, or only read one line of input.

tasks.fb: A parameter is the name the procedure gives to whatever is handed to it. The value you pass in when you call it is the argument.

teach.say: A parameter is a name in the brackets of the def line. Whatever you pass in when you call it arrives under that name.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers, one on each line. Write a procedure called product that takes both numbers and prints total [the first times the second]. Call product once.
brief: The procedure does the printing, not the main program.
One space after the word total.

tests.why: 4 times 75 is 300. If you got total 475 you joined the two inputs as text instead of turning them into numbers with int().
One times anything is that number. A multiplication that works only here usually means the arguments were passed the wrong way round.
Nothing times 50 is 0, and the procedure still has to print a line. Printing nothing at all for this case is a common slip.
Bigger numbers must work too. If this failed but the others passed, you may have typed a fixed answer into the procedure.

tasks.fb: Two parameters are separated by a comma in the def line, and the arguments go in the same order when you call it. Order matters, not the names.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Write a function called double that returns twice its parameter. Display [what double hands back] and nothing else.
brief: The number may be negative or zero.
One line of output, holding the number and nothing else.
tasks.starter: # double returns, it does not print

tests.why: Double 7 is 14. If nothing was printed, your function returns the answer but the main program never printed it.
Double zero is zero, and it still has to be printed.
Negative numbers double too. If you used a loop that adds, it may not run for a negative value.
If this one failed, check you used int(input()) - doubling the text 250 as text gives 250250.

tasks.fb: return hands a value back to whatever called the function, so print(double(7)) prints 14. Without return the function hands back None.

teach.say: return hands a value back to the line that called the function, so the caller is the one that prints or stores it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Write a function called sign that returns the word up for a number above 0. Make sign return down for a number below 0. Make sign return flat for 0. Display [what sign hands back] and nothing else.
brief: sign holds no print of its own.
Print exactly one of: up, down, flat
tasks.starter: # a function can hand back a word

tests.why: Above 0, so the word handed back is up. Nothing printed at all means the function returns it but the main program never printed it.
Below 0 gives down. A function with only one return works for one case and hands back None for the rest.
Exactly 0 is neither above nor below, so it is flat. This is the case a > and < pair always forgets.
A large number is still only up. If this crashed, check you used int(input()) - text comparisons would not sort it.
One below 0 is still down, so the test has to be against 0 rather than against 1.

tasks.fb: A function can hand back text just as easily as a number, and return stops the function the moment it runs - so the lines after it never happen.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers, one on each line. Write a function called area that returns the first times the second. Store what area returns in a variable. Display one line in the form area [that value].
brief: area holds no print at all.
A single space goes after the word area.
Store the returned value in a variable before you print it.
tasks.starter: # store the returned value before printing it

tests.why: One line only. If you got an extra line with 20 on its own, your function printed the answer as well as returning it - that is the mistake this question is about.
One times one is 1. If the line read area None, the function printed the answer instead of returning it, so there was nothing to hand back.
A second number of 0 gives 0, and the line must still be printed.
If only the first test passed, you may have written the answer into the function rather than calculating it from the parameters.

tasks.fb: Printing and returning are not the same thing. A function that prints shows the value once and throws it away; a function that returns gives it to the caller, which can store it, add to it or print it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a word. Then ask for a whole number. Write a function called tag that returns high for a number of 40 or more. Make tag return low for a number below 40. Write a procedure called show that displays [word]: [the word tag handed back]. Use both subprograms to print that one line.
brief: A colon and one space separate the word from the answer.
tasks.starter: # tag returns a word, show prints the line

tests.why: 55 is 40 or more, so the answer is high, and the procedure does the printing. Two lines of output means tag printed as well as returned.
Exactly 40 is high. Getting low here means you tested > 40 instead of >= 40.
39 is under 40. If this printed high, your function may be returning a value only on one branch and None otherwise.
A number of 0 is still a number and must be reported. Crashing here usually means int() was never used on the second input.

tasks.fb: OCR asks for the difference by name: a function returns a value, a procedure does not. In this program tag is the function and show is the procedure, and the program needs both.

teach.say: A function ends with return and hands a value back; a procedure only prints. So a function's answer can be passed straight into a procedure.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers, one on each line. Write a function called larger that returns the bigger of its two parameters. Write a procedure called announce that displays largest [that value]. Use both subprograms to print that one line.
brief: When the two numbers are equal, that value is the larger.
larger holds no print of its own.
One space after the word largest.
tasks.starter: # larger works it out, announce prints it

tests.why: The first number is the bigger one here. If nothing printed, larger returns the answer but announce was never called with it.
The same two numbers the other way round, so a function that always returns its first parameter fails here.
Equal numbers, so that value is the answer. A function that only returns on one branch hands back None here.
With negatives the bigger number is the one closer to 0, so -8 is the answer rather than -20.
Two zeros still have an answer, and the line still has to be printed.

tasks.fb: larger works the answer out and hands it back; announce only prints. Keeping the two jobs apart is exactly what the words function and procedure mean.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Keep it in a variable called total. Write a procedure called boost with a local total of its own, set to 99. Make boost print its own total. Call boost. Then display [the main total] on the next line.
brief: The main program's total must not change.

tests.why: The 5 survives. If the second line also says 99, you wrote global total inside the procedure, so it changed the main program's variable instead of making a local one.
Zero is still the main program's value afterwards.
If this crashed, check you used int(input()) - a minus sign is fine for int but not for a text comparison.
If the second line printed 99 only on some tests, the procedure is printing after the main program rather than before. Call boost first, then print.

tasks.fb: A variable created inside a subprogram is local: it exists only while the subprogram runs and disappears afterwards. The main program's total is a different variable that happens to share a name.

teach.say: A name given a value inside a subprogram is local and vanishes when the subprogram ends. To change a variable from outside instead, the subprogram must say global first.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Keep it in a variable called count. Write a procedure called bump that takes one whole number. Make bump add 1 to its parameter. Make bump print the result. Call bump with count. Then display [count] on the next line.
brief: count itself must not change, because a parameter is a copy.
tasks.starter: # the parameter is a copy, not the variable itself

tests.why: 6 then 5. If the second line says 6 as well, you changed count itself rather than the parameter inside the procedure.
One more than 0 is 1, and count is still 0 afterwards.
Adding 1 to a negative number moves it up towards 0, and count is unchanged. A crash here means int() was never used.
If the two lines came out the other way round, the printing inside bump happens after the main program's line - call bump first.

tasks.fb: A parameter is a local name holding a copy of the value, so adding to it inside the subprogram leaves the caller's variable exactly as it was.

tasks.q: Write a procedure called up that adds 3 to a shared total. Write a procedure called down that adds 1 to the same total. Ask the user for a whole number of turns. Call up and then down once per turn. Display [the final total] and nothing else.
brief: That 0 is fixed in the program, not typed in.
The total is shared by the whole program.
A number of 0 turns means neither procedure is called.
tasks.starter: # up and down change the main program's total

tests.why: One turn is 3 plus 1. If you got 0, the procedures made their own local total instead of changing the main program's - they need global total.
Five turns at 4 each. Getting 4 means the total is being set back to 0 somewhere inside the loop or inside a procedure.
If this gave 9 or 3, only one of the two procedures is being called inside the loop.
No turns, so nothing is added and the starting 0 is printed. A program that prints something else here never handled the loop running zero times.

tasks.fb: A global variable is one the whole program can see. A subprogram may read it without saying anything, but to change it the subprogram must declare global first, or Python makes a local copy instead.

tasks.q: Write a function called score that returns 3 for a number of 2 or more. Make score return 1 for a number of 1. Make score return 0 for 0. Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers, one on each line. Add up everything score hands back. Display [that total] and nothing else.
brief: Call score once per number, inside the loop.
There may be none at all.
tasks.starter: # one call per number, added to a running total

tests.why: 3 plus 1 plus 0 is 4. If you got 3, the total is being replaced each time round the loop instead of added to.
A 5 is still just 3, because the function returns 3 for anything from 2 upwards.
No numbers at all, so the loop never runs and the total is still 0. The program must still print a line. Crashing here means you read a number before checking how many there were.
Two zeros and two ones. If this crashed with an input error, your loop is reading more lines than it was told there were.
Two numbers of 2 are worth 3 each. If the total came out as 3, the function is being called once outside the loop rather than once per number.

tasks.fb: Calling a subprogram inside a loop is how one piece of code gets reused on every item. The loop deals with how many times; the function deals with one number at a time.

teach.say: What a function returns is an ordinary value, so it can be added up. Called inside a loop, it runs once per turn.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers, one on each line. Write a function called base that returns the first number times 25. Write a function called whole that calls base. Make whole return what base gave times the second number, plus 10. Write a procedure called report that calls whole. Make report display first [the first number]. Then make report display whole [that value] on the next line.
brief: Two lines of output, in that order.
The 10 is added after the multiplying, not before.
tasks.starter: # report calls whole, whole calls base

tests.why: 2 times 25 is 50, times 3 is 150, plus 10 is 160. Getting 60 means the 10 was added before multiplying by the second number.
25 for the first number, times 1, plus 10. If the second line said whole None, whole prints instead of returning, so report had nothing to print.
A first number of 0 still leaves the 10. A program that skips the whole calculation when it is 0 prints the wrong thing here.
125 for the first number, times 2, plus 10. If this failed, check whole is calling base rather than repeating the times 25 itself.

tasks.fb: Subprograms can call subprograms. report calls whole, whole calls base, and each one only has to know its own job - that is how a big program is broken into small ones.

tasks.q: Is each subprogram a function or a procedure?
items: Works out an area and returns it
Returns pass or fail for a mark
Returns the total of a list
tasks.fb: If a value comes back it is a function. If it only does a job, it is a procedure.

info.title: Why bother
info.text: A job written once and called from four places is tested once and fixed once. The same lines copied four times are four bugs waiting to happen.

info.title: Default values
info.text: A parameter can be given a default, so label("Juice") still works when the price is usually the same.

info.title: Returning more
info.text: return can hand back several values at once, separated by commas, and the caller unpacks them.

info.title: Already written
info.text: len(), int() and round() are functions somebody else wrote: you call them exactly the way you call your own.

info.title: Globals are risky
info.text: Any subprogram can change a global, so one bug can break all of them. Parameters and return values are safer.

info.title: Calling itself
info.text: A subprogram is even allowed to call itself. That is called recursion, and it is how a merge sort splits a list.
